phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], exactly the English m; the name opens on the same sound as the place-name Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) from which it descends.
The Welsh clear y, an unstressed-quality central vowel [ə] — the 'uh' of English 'about' — because it stands in the stressed penult.
Voiced dental fricative [ð], the soft 'th' of English 'this'; Welsh writes the sound with the digraph dd, and it never hardens to a stop.
Final unstressed syllable with the Welsh final-y sound [ɨ], a high central vowel between the i of 'bit' and the Welsh u, closing on [n].

pronunciation.approximation: 'MUR-thin' — stress the first syllable (the Welsh penult); the dd is the soft 'th' of 'this', and the whole name takes two short beats, never 'MER-lin'.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Myrddin, the prophet and wild man of the Black Book of Carmarthen and the Red Book of Hergest; son of Morfryn in the Welsh Triads.

kin.label: Medieval Latin
kin.form: Merlinus — Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latinization (Historia Regum Britanniae, c. 1136; Vita Merlini, c. 1150), the form that conquered the world.

kin.label: Welsh epithets
kin.form: Myrddin Wyllt, 'Myrddin the Wild'; Myrddin Emrys, the Ambrosian prophet of Dinas Emrys.

kin.label: Name origin
kin.form: From the place-name Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen), itself from Roman Moridunum, 'sea-fort' — the person is named from the place, not the place from the person.

pronunciation.note: Myrddin is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose, and the digraph dd is an orthographic convention, not a lost character. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the prophet's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Wild Prophet of the Forest
domains.subtitle: Seer, Wild Man
domains.lead: Myrddin is the original Welsh form of the name the world knows as Merlin: the prophet who went mad at the battle of Arfderydd in 573, fled into the Caledonian forest, and lived there as a wild man — lamenting his dead lord Gwenddolau, sheltering beneath an apple tree, and uttering the prophecies that made him the canonical voice of Welsh vaticination before Geoffrey of Monmouth made him the wizard of the Arthurian world.

cards.name: The Apple Tree
cards.desc: The sweet apple tree that shelters Myrddin in the Afallennau — his only house in the forest of Celyddon, addressed like a friend.

cards.name: Arfderydd
cards.desc: The northern battle of 573 where his lord Gwenddolau son of Ceidio fell; grief and slaughter drove Myrddin mad, says the Welsh Triad.

cards.name: The Threefold Death
cards.desc: The death Myrddin prophesies in the Vita Merlini — from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — fulfilled to the letter; the wild prophet's own end in the northern tale.

cards.name: The Brud
cards.desc: The prophetic poems gathered under his name — the Black Book's Afallennau and Oianau, and Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini, the most copied political prophecy of the Middle Ages.

symbols.name: The apple tree
symbols.meaning: The wild man's shelter and confidant — prophecy spoken from hiding, sweet and bitter at once

symbols.name: The forest of Celyddon
symbols.meaning: The Caledonian wood — madness, exile, and second sight in one landscape

symbols.name: The stag
symbols.meaning: The wild mount he rides to court in the Vita Merlini, driving the forest's herds before him

symbols.name: Rock, tree, and water
symbols.meaning: The three elements of the foretold death — prophecy that cannot miss, however it is guarded against

symbols.name: Gwenddydd's questions
symbols.meaning: The sister's dialogue — prophecy as the speech left between the mad and those who loved them

mythology.lead: Myrddin's dossier divides in two, and the tradition itself knew it: the northern prophet who went mad at Arfderydd and fled to Coed Celyddon, preserved in the Welsh Triads, the Annales Cambriae, and the Black Book poems; and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Merlinus, who carried the wild man into Latin and grafted him onto the Arthurian world. Gerald of Wales already separated them in the twelfth century: Merlinus Ambrosius, the boy prophet of Vortigern's tower, and Merlinus Celidonius — Sylvester — the wild man of the Caledonian forest.

myths.title: The Battle of Arfderydd
myths.text:
The Annales Cambriae enter under the year 573 the battle of Arfderydd, fought in the north between the sons of Eliffer and Gwenddolau son of Ceidio — a historical-seeming conflict of the British Old North. The Welsh Triads count it among the futile battles of the Island of Britain, brought about, in the triad's famous understatement, for a lark's nest; and the triad records the consequence that matters here: Gwenddolau fell, and Myrddin became mad.

From that seed the whole legend grows. Myrddin son of Morfryn, his lord dead and his side defeated, flees the world of the mead-hall into Coed Celyddon, the Caledonian forest, and becomes Myrddin Wyllt — the Wild — living from the forest's gifts and speaking only in verse and prophecy.

myths.title: The Apple Trees and the Oianau
myths.text:
The earliest Welsh manuscript, the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), preserves the poems that give the wild man his own voice. In Yr Afallennau, 'The Apple Trees', Myrddin addresses the sweet apple tree that shelters him: he laments Gwenddolau, slain in the bloodshed of Arfderydd; he grieves that he endures want while once he rode at the head of warriors; he hides from Rhydderch's men; and the refrain returns to the tree, his one companion and hiding-place.

The companion poem, Yr Oianau, keeps the same voice — the outcast prophet calling his mournful 'oian' through the forest, mourning his dead, marked out by madness as the gods' or fate's chosen sufferer. These are not narrative poems but laments with prophecy threaded through them; together they made Myrddin the patron and mouthpiece of the whole Welsh prophetic genre.

myths.title: The Conversation of Myrddin and Gwenddydd
myths.text:
The Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei chwaer — 'The Conversation of Myrddin and His Sister Gwenddydd' — is the tradition's most human document. Gwenddydd, wife of Rhydderch and sister of the wild prophet, questions her brother across the gulf his madness has opened: she mourns the warrior he was, the mead-feasts he no longer honours, the lord they both have lost. Myrddin answers her with prophecy — the fate of Wales, the coming of its deliverers — but the prophecy keeps breaking against grief.

The dialogue fixes what the poems imply: the wild man is not forsaken but watched from the world he left. Gwenddydd survives in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin as Ganieda — Rhydderch's queen, Myrddin's sister, and, at the end of the Vita Merlini, his successor in prophecy itself.

myths.title: The Threefold Death and the Life of the Forest
myths.text:
Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini (c. 1150) is the wild man's fullest biography. Merlinus — poet, prophet, and king in Geoffrey's telling — loses his reason at a battle among the northern princes and flees to the Caledonian wood, where he lives as a silvester homo, a man of the forest, feeding on roots and fruit, snow on his shoulders, unknown to his own court. Rhydderch's men find him and drag him back; at court he laughs at things no one understands, and his laughter is always a prophecy. To a boy he foretells a threefold death: from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — and the boy, falling from a cliff, is caught by a tree with his head in the stream, dying all three deaths at once, as no human prudence could have guarded against.

The poem lets him go home to the forest at last. He appears riding a stag, driving the woodland herds before him like a shepherd of the wild; [[taliesin|Taliesin]] — Telgesinus in the Latin — comes to him, and the two seers discourse at length on the winds, the waters, the fishes, and the making of the world. In the end Merlin gives his observatory to his sister Ganieda, who takes up the prophetic gift, and retires to the forest for good — the mad king become the wise wild man, the only sovereignty he can still keep.

myths.title: The Boy at Vortigern's Tower
myths.text:
Geoffrey's other Merlin came from another book. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum of Nennius tells of the boy Ambrosius — a child without a father — brought to King Vortigern to be sacrificed so that his collapsing tower at Dinas Emrys might stand; the boy instead reveals the pool beneath the foundations and the two dragons, red and white, whose battle is the prophecy of Britain: the red dragon of the Britons, the white of the Saxons.

Geoffrey took Nennius's boy and gave him Myrddin's name: Merlinus Ambrosius. The graft made one figure of two traditions — the royal prophet of the tower and the mad prophet of the forest — and Gerald of Wales, a generation later, was already insisting they were two. The composite Merlin who results is the one the world inherited: prophet to Vortigern, architect of kings, and, in the romances that followed, counsellor of Arthur himself.

lore.syncretism: Myrddin's comparisons run north, not east. The twelfth-century Life of St Kentigern by Jocelyn of Furness knows a mad prophet at the court of Rhydderch Hael named Lailoken, who foretold his own threefold death; a fragmentary Latin life of 'Merlin the Wild' preserved in the Cotton collection tells the same penitence, conversion by Kentigern, and triple end — stoned, fallen on a stake, drowned in the Tweed. Nikolai Tolstoy's Quest for Merlin argued that Lailoken and Myrddin Wyllt are two records of one north-British wild-man figure, and the modern handbooks treat the kinship as real, its exact shape unproven. The Irish tradition offers no namesake — the wild men of the Irish tales, Suibhne Geilt above all, share the type rather than the name: the king driven mad by battle who lives in trees, speaks in verse, and is watched by the court he left. Within the Welsh corpus his truest kin is [[taliesin|Taliesin]], the other great prophetic poet, with whom the Vita Merlini pairs him in discourse; and his own tradition split him in two, as Gerald of Wales records — Merlinus Ambrosius of Dinas Emrys and Merlinus Celidonius of the Caledonian forest, the tower-boy and the wild man the romances later fused.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Celtic figure has had a stranger second life. Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini — the seventh book of the Historia — circulated separately for centuries and became the most copied political prophecy of the Latin Middle Ages, mined for omens by kings and rebels alike; the romances then turned the prophet into the enchanter, and by the thirteenth-century Vulgate cycle Merlin is Arthur's maker: arranger of Uther's night at Tintagel, keeper of the Round Table's founding, and prisoner of the Lady of the Lake. Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49) and the nineteenth-century Arthurian revival carried the Welsh roots back into English view, and modern scholarship — Jarman above all — rebuilt the northern prophet behind the wizard. In Welsh memory the original never disappeared: Caerfyrddin, 'Myrddin's fortress', still bears the folk etymology Geoffrey loved, and the Myrddin of the Black Book remains the patron of Welsh prophecy — the figure every later brud quietly pretended to be. The name now means the wizard worldwide; the temple's task is to hand the name back to the wild man it began with.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Myrddin is the figure who paid for knowledge with the ordinary world. Every version of him loses something before he sees: a lord, a battle, his reason, his hall. The tradition is strikingly honest about the transaction — the prophecy is real, and so is the madness, and the same event, the slaughter at Arfderydd, gives him both. He is the answer Celtic literature gives to the question of what a seer is: not a priest with a technique but a survivor whom grief has put outside the human settlement, close enough to the trees that the future can get a word in. His sister comes to the edge of the forest to ask what will happen; he tells her, and stays. That is the shape of the gift — the future, at the price of the present.

And his name tells the same story in miniature. It is not a theonym but a place-name: Caerfyrddin, the sea-fort, Moridunum, given to a man. The wild prophet carries a fortress in his name — the ordered world he was driven out of, remembered every time anyone calls him.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Myrddin — attested in the Black Book of Carmarthen (NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250, the earliest Welsh manuscript) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), and in the Welsh Triads. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the restoration to recover — the digraph dd for the soft 'th' is orthography, not a lost character — which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: myrddin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Myrddin is a textual figure, and his witnesses are among the most precisely identified in Welsh letters. The Afallennau and Oianau stand in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250), the earliest surviving manuscript in Welsh; the Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd stands in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410); Geoffrey's Vita Merlini survives complete in a single manuscript (British Library, Cotton Vespasian E.iv, thirteenth century). The landscape behind the texts is real and partly recoverable: Arfderydd is traditionally identified with Arthuret near Longtown in Cumbria, in the Old North the poems remember; Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) overlays the Roman fort of Moridunum, 'sea-fort', attested in the Antonine Itinerary and confirmed by excavation — the place-name from which, on the scholarly account, the prophet's name derives; and Dinas Emrys, the hillfort in Gwynedd where Nennius sets the fatherless boy and the dragons, yielded post-Roman occupation material in Savory's excavations of 1954–56. No inscription names Myrddin, and none would be expected: the early stones of Wales record the dead, not prophets.
